Archival collection and chronology, microscopy, independent laboratory funds; distinguish institutional commemoration from primary documents.
Childhood and family, medicine, Cuba, academic career and art; contemporary award institution text with historical biographical narrative.
Original argument for individuality and contiguity, spinal roots, retinal circuits, cerebellum, dynamic polarization; not a modern microscopy study.
Golgi rejects neuron doctrine, continues reticular position even while sharing award with Cajal.
1887 staining, 1888 papers, Berlin, laboratory, Junta, lineage of Spanish histologists and independence of subsequent research.
Detailed career, life and publication chronology; cross-check less precise recollections with archival institutional dates.
Memoir in multiple revised editions; childhood artist/mischief/barber/shoemaker, family tensions, war and illness: recollection not contemporary transcript.
Marriage in 1879, seven children, Silveria Fañanás household and photochemical/histological practical assistance, family photography.
Nobel award attribution, 1873 Golgi invention, 1906 lectures, Cajal multivolume research and Nobel committee division; based on Nobel archival documents.
Historical reticular theory versus cell individuality; shared Nobel legacy and the separate contributions of the scientists.
Simarro demonstrated Golgi preparations in 1887; technical reception and modifications; chemical stain and morphology.
Retinal contributions, competing neural theories, Golgi stain and 1906 prize.
Simarro role, 1888 results, 1889 Kölliker, dynamic polarization, plasticity interpretation; distinguish Cajal from modern biochemical confirmation.
Growth cones, neurotropic hypothesis, 1888–1893 studies, 1905–08 regeneration, 1910–14 experimental guidance, not later discovery of nerve growth factor.
Late peripheral nerve regeneration studies; relationship between anatomical individuality and sprouting; Golgi group’s parallel research.
Distinct roles of Nicolás Achúcarro and Río-Hortega in discovery of microglia and oligodendrocytes; relation to Spanish school.
1920 break between Cajal and Río-Hortega, autonomous laboratory in Residencia de Estudiantes, linked to Achúcarro.
Cajal’s detailed cortical neuroanatomy and Golgi-method studies of late 1880s and early 1890s.
Modern appraisal of scientific drawings and impact, secondary context; contains a historically incorrect date for Golgi’s stain (use 1873 from Golgi/Nobel scholarship instead).
